checkpoints: Feedback latency (time-to-first-signal) matters more than total wall-clock in a CI pipeline; running lint last means the cheapest, most common failure surfaces slowest, at minute ~20-24 instead of within a minute of pushing.

Cheap, deterministic checks like lint should run ahead of expensive, flaky ones like E2E — ordering steps by cost gives fast fail signals without forcing every failure to wait behind the longest suite.

Splitting a single serial job into independent jobs — lint, unit, e2e — triggered by the same event lets the CI platform schedule them onto separate runners in parallel, collapsing wall-clock from the sum of all steps (~25 min) down to roughly the longest leg (~15 min for e2e).
Decoupling the checks into separate jobs also means a flaky e2e rerun no longer forces lint and unit to rerun alongside it, since they are independent rather than sequential steps inside one job.

`actions/setup-node@v4`'s `cache: 'npm'` option (or an explicit `actions/cache@v4` step) keyed on `hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')` caches the `~/.npm` store rather than `node_modules` itself, so `npm ci`'s integrity check still runs on install while avoiding a fully cold download every time.

Adding a restore-keys prefix — the cache key string with the trailing hash portion dropped — lets a near-miss, such as a single dependency bump, still restore most of the store instead of falling back to a completely cold install.

Matrixing jobs across multiple Node versions (e.g. 18, 20, 22) multiplies version coverage at roughly the wall-clock cost of a single leg, because matrix legs run in parallel rather than being multiplied serially; the real trade-off is paid in more concurrent runner minutes, not in extra wall-clock time.

A redesign like this should be verified concretely: comparing before/after run durations, timing a deliberately lint-broken commit to confirm a fast first-failure, checking the cache-hit line in the setup-node step's log, and confirming in the Actions tab that the matrix legs actually run concurrently rather than queuing one after another.
